# **Architectural Protocols and Empirical Foundations for Self-Evolving Agent Workspaces**

## **Paradigm Shift: The Workspace as an Executable Cognitive Harness**

Autonomous software engineering agents are undergoing a structural shift from prompt-centric wrappers to executable cognitive harnesses1. Historically, attempts to improve agent capability relied on accumulating natural-language instructions within central configuration files such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, expanding context windows, or adding unconstrained memory stores3. Empirical evidence reveals that unmanaged instruction growth induces context bloat, degrades model attention, and increases regression risk without improving end-to-end task completion rates3. Modern agent engineering redefines the workspace as an explicit, observable, and permissioned environment that surrounds a frozen language model inference core1.
In this harness-centric model, the language model operates exclusively as a reasoning engine, while the surrounding workspace manages state tracking, context selection, tool execution, structural constraint enforcement, automated verification, permission gating, failure attribution, and trajectory logging2. When an agent encounters repeated execution failures or requires frequent human correction, categorizing the failure as a knowledge deficit solvable by adding textual instructions is fundamentally flawed2. Systemic evaluations demonstrate that a significant proportion of apparent model failures originate in infrastructure deficiencies—including non-deterministic tool outputs, ambiguous directory layouts, unverified state transitions, broad permission boundaries, or opaque execution logs2.
The primary objective of workspace self-improvement is not to maximize instructions, tools, or autonomous actions5. Instead, self-improvement protocols optimize for minimizing repeated errors, human interventions, unnecessary decision points, context token burden, and regression risks3. An effective remodeling effort frequently simplifies the workspace by replacing natural-language instructions with deterministic environmental constraints, automated check scripts, and encapsulated execution wrappers3.

## **Configuration Smells and Architectural Friction in Workspace Manifests**

Empirical repository mining of open-source agent environments demonstrates that persistent configuration files rapidly accumulate structural anti-patterns, termed configuration smells3. An analysis of open-source repositories utilizing open-agent instruction files revealed that 91% contained at least one named configuration defect5. These defects degrade model performance by consuming always-loaded context space, introducing contradictory behavioral priors, and diverting model attention away from critical project constraints5.

| Configuration Smell | Empirical Prevalence | Core Architectural Mechanism | Systemic Impact and Failure Mode | Remediation Protocol |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Lint Leakage** | 62% | Re-stating deterministic formatting, naming, or style rules in text instruction files5. | Wastes always-loaded context space on constraints that pre-commit hooks or linters enforce deterministically for free3. | Offload style enforcement entirely to static analysis tools (e.g., Ruff, Biome)5. |
| **Context Bloat** | 42% | Configuration files exceeding structural length thresholds (e.g., \>200 lines)5. | Exceeds the token boundary where models reliably attend to rules, inducing instruction suppression5. | Modularize configuration; split specialized rules into on-demand skills3. |
| **Skill Leakage** | 35% | Embedding specialized, low-frequency procedure guides inside global configuration files5. | Injects domain-specific rules into every session, competing with core project instructions5. | Extract procedural guides into dedicated skill artifacts loaded conditionally5. |
| **Conflicting Instructions** | 28% | Preserving contradictory, stale, or mutually exclusive behavioral guidelines5. | Induces model hesitation, looping, or arbitrary preference selection under ambiguous instructions5. | Deploy automated contradiction detectors; establish single-source-of-truth guidelines5. |
| **Init Fossilization** | 24% | Retaining boilerplate context generated by automated initialization tools without editing5. | Pollutes the context with generic assumptions unaligned with actual project realities5. | Audit initialization files; strip unverified placeholder directives5. |
| **Blind References** | 16% | Referencing external file paths or documentation directories without scope explanations5. | Causes models to randomly parse massive external files or ignore vital contextual paths5. | Annotate file paths with explicit usage criteria and contextual relevance pitches5. |

Statistical co-occurrence analysis reveals that configuration defects compound one another5. The simultaneous presence of Skill Leakage and Conflicting Instructions increases the empirical probability of severe Context Bloat by 83%4. Furthermore, benchmark evaluations on SWE-bench Lite and AGENTbench confirm that unmanaged, LLM-generated context files reduce task success by 3% while increasing inference costs by 20%4. Consequently, self-improving workspace protocols must treat instruction manifests as minimal, audited entry points rather than historical logs of agent experience5.

## **Empirical Research Synthesis: State-of-the-Art Self-Improvement Paradigms**

To establish a defensible, evidence-based remodeling strategy, the workspace must draw upon modern advancements in skill optimization, harness evolution, and joint adaptation1. Recent literature provides rigorous frameworks that replace loose self-revision with controlled, gradient-like text-space updates1.

### **SkillOpt: Gradient-Descent Analogies in Text-Space Optimization**

SkillOpt reframes natural-language skill documents as trainable external state variables ![][image1] governing a frozen language model target ![][image2]1. Rather than rewriting entire instruction documents in an unconstrained manner, SkillOpt executes a structured forward-backward-update cycle across task batches5:

* **Forward Rollout**: The frozen agent executes a batch of training tasks using the current skill document ![][image3], capturing full interaction trajectories, tool calls, and verifier scores1.
* **Minibatch Reflection**: A distinct frontier optimizer model analyzes rollouts, categorizing outcomes into four discrete groups: Improvements, Regressions, Persistent Failures, and Stable Successes5.
* **Bounded Text Updates**: The optimizer proposes structured, localized edits (Add, Delete, Replace) restricted by a textual learning-rate edit budget ![][image4] to prevent sweeping semantic jumps1.
* **Validation Gating and Memory**: Every candidate skill document ![][image5] must pass a strict validation gate on a held-out evaluation dataset1. Edits are adopted only if they yield monotonic score improvements1. Rejected updates are appended to a negative knowledge buffer, providing explicit feedback to guide future optimization steps5.
* **Epoch-Wise Slow/Meta Updates**: Long-horizon consolidation synthesizes multi-epoch learnings into compact, high-density rules without expanding token length1.

Across 52 distinct evaluation settings covering direct chat, Codex, and Claude Code execution loops, SkillOpt achieved superior or tied performance in 100% of benchmark configurations1. On procedural benchmarks such as SpreadsheetBench, SkillOpt lifted GPT-5.5 accuracy from 41.8% to 80.7% while introducing zero inference-time token overhead during deployment1.

### **Trace2Skill: Inductive Parallel Distillation over Execution Traces**

Complementing SkillOpt's optimization loop, Trace2Skill introduces a parallel trajectory distillation framework designed to author portable, multi-file skill directories ![][image6], where ![][image7] represents the root SKILL.md file and ![][image8] contains supporting scripts, templates, and reference assets6.
Rather than modifying skills sequentially based on single trajectories—which risks severe overfitting to local context—Trace2Skill dispatches parallel fleets of specialized analyst sub-agents6:

* **Agentic Error Analysts (![][image9])**: Inspect failure traces ![][image10] within an interactive loop, executing diagnostic tools against intermediate artifacts to uncover exact causal mechanisms rather than speculative errors7.
* **Success Analysts (![][image11])**: Analyze successful traces ![][image12] to isolate high-efficiency operational patterns and optimal tool invocation chains7.

A central consolidation engine applies inductive reasoning to merge candidate patches into a conflict-free directory, eliminating redundant rules and verifying that newly introduced standard operating procedures do not degrade existing model capabilities7. Trace2Skill demonstrates that procedural knowledge distilled from trajectories transfers cleanly across model scales (e.g., from 35B parameter models to 122B parameter models) and between entirely different model families without parameter updates or test-time retrieval modules6.

### **Online Harness Evolution and Joint Adaptation: Evo-Harness, HarnessEvolve, and WHALE**

Extending optimization beyond text-based skill files, recent frameworks investigate the continuous adaptation of the executable harness itself.
Evo-Harness establishes an online harness learning protocol where execution contexts ![][image13] from task streams are continually compiled into structured harness entries ![][image14]. An evolver module extracts topic-level procedures and planning abstractions, injecting a budgeted subset ![][image15] into future task contexts.
HarnessEvolve addresses systemic instability in evolving environments by isolating credit assignment, preventing task-specific shortcut learning, and guarding against catastrophic forgetting through held-out reference trajectory evaluation.
Weight-Harness Alternating LEarning (WHALE) reveals a fundamental coupling between model parameters and executable harness code. WHALE proves that optimizing either weights or harness code in isolation leads to performance bottlenecks; updating model capability changes which harness structures are optimal, and altering harness control flow shifts which model capabilities are exposed. By alternating between online rejection-sampling fine-tuning and Meta-Harness updates under adaptive patience rules, WHALE achieves performance gains of \+4.15 to \+24.38 percentage points over single-axis adaptation strategies.

| Paradigm / Framework | Primary Target State | Core Update Mechanism | Validation & Gating Mechanism | Deployment Overhead | Generalization & Transfer |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **SkillOpt** \[cite: 1, 5\] | Single skill document (SKILL.md)1. | Bounded Add/Delete/Replace edits with learning rate budget ![][image4]9. | Strict held-out validation gate; rejected edit buffer9. | Zero extra tokens or API calls at runtime1. | High transfer across model scales and agentic harnesses1. |
| **Trace2Skill** \[cite: 6\] | Modular skill tree ![][image16]. | Parallel trace collection; ReAct error & success analysis6. | Hierarchical conflict-free consolidation7. | Zero runtime retrieval or parameter overhead6. | High cross-family and out-of-distribution transfer7. |
| **Evo-Harness** \[cite: \] | External context harness ![][image14]. | Context-to-harness compilation from execution streams. | Injection budget constraints and evolver reflection. | Minor context injection budget ![][image17]. | Topic-level and domain-level continuous adaptation. |
| **WHALE** \[cite: \] | Joint weights ![][image18] and harness code ![][image14]. | Alternating rejection-sampling fine-tuning & Meta-Harness search. | Adaptive patience rules over training signals. | Variable dependent on harness modifications. | High intra-domain optimization efficiency. |

## **Phase-Based Remodeling Execution Protocol**

To prevent unconstrained agent drift, workspace self-improvement must follow an explicit, multi-phase execution protocol. An agent must never begin by rewriting core configuration files or adding speculative instructions. The remodeling process strictly separates investigation, inventory, friction analysis, baseline measurement, and hypothesis-driven experimentation.
The execution flow advances sequentially through five mandatory operational phases:

> 1. **Phase 0**: Establish Remodeling Boundaries & Isolation.
> 2. **Phase 1**: Inventory Workspace Components & Map Architecture.
> 3. **Phase 2**: Identify & Classify Operational Friction.
> 4. **Phase 3**: Measure Baseline Telemetry & Metrics.
> 5. **Phase 4**: Perform Targeted Research & Formulate Hypotheses.

### **Phase 0 — Establishing Remodeling Boundaries and Isolation**

Before inspecting or altering any workspace component, the agent must establish strict system boundaries and permission models8:

* **Workspace Scope**: Identify the exact root directory and directory tree governing the session.
* **Authority Classification**: Classify all files into Authoritative (human-managed source rules), Generated (produced by build tools or agents), Disposable (cache, temporary execution outputs), and Protected (files the agent must never modify automatically, such as security policies or root hooks).
* **Permission Isolation**: Define which tools possess write access, which execution scripts require sandboxing, and where experimental candidate changes can be isolated (e.g., git worktrees or dedicated test branches) and cleanly reverted upon validation failure2.

### **Phase 1 — Workspace Inventory and Architectural Mapping**

The agent must construct a complete inventory of workspace components. Each identified component must be audited against a standardized specification schema:
![][image19]
The agent builds a conceptual architecture map contrasting intended control flow against actual directory structures, identifying where execution flow diverges from formal documentation8.

### **Phase 2 — Friction Identification and Taxonomy**

The workspace must be thoroughly scanned for concrete evidence of operational friction5. Rather than relying on speculative assessments, the agent identifies friction signals through specific indicators: repeated TODO markers, manual recovery comments, duplicated instructional logic across files, stale documentation, shell scripts repeatedly invoked by human operators, failed local test runs, and repetitive error-handling traces2.
Every identified friction item is assigned to exactly one of eleven functional domains:

> 1. **Knowledge**: Missing domain concepts or business logic.
> 2. **Retrieval**: Failure to discover or load existing relevant documentation or skills5.
> 3. **Tool**: Missing, fragile, or non-deterministic execution wrappers8.
> 4. **Workflow**: Absence of automated sequencing for complex multi-step tasks.
> 5. **Structure**: Ambiguous directory layouts or missing standard entry points8.
> 6. **Verification**: Lack of deterministic pass/fail checks or hidden test suites2.
> 7. **Observability**: Opaque failure outputs lacking actionable error diagnostics8.
> 8. **Permission**: Excessively strict or broadly ambiguous tool access boundaries8.
> 9. **State/Memory**: Unmanaged session state leakage or context accumulation2.
> 10. **Human Judgment**: Tasks fundamentally requiring subjective human decisions.
> 11. **Unknown**: Uncategorized or non-reproducible operational anomalies.

### **Phase 3 — Baseline Measurement and Metric Instrumentation**

Remodeling must be governed by quantitative metrics. Prior to introducing workspace edits, the agent attempts to measure baseline performance across ten key indicators:
![][image20]
If historical task telemetry is unavailable, the baseline for these metrics must be explicitly logged as UNKNOWN. In this scenario, the initial remodeling phase must focus exclusively on instrumenting telemetry mechanisms rather than modifying cognitive or operational logic8.

### **Phase 4 — Targeted Mechanism Research**

The agent conducts targeted research into specific architectural mechanisms to resolve identified friction points. For every researched pattern, the agent evaluates reported empirical results, limitations, and relevance to the target workspace, categorizing evidence into four rigor tiers:

* **Grade A**: Replicated, peer-reviewed empirical evidence across multiple models and benchmarks1.
* **Grade B**: Credible experimental evidence in controlled benchmark studies3.
* **Grade C**: Promising framework proposals with limited empirical replication.
* **Grade D**: Conceptual ideas, unverified blog posts, or speculative claims.

The agent explicitly distinguishes between established facts ("researchers proved this mechanism works") and local hypotheses ("this mechanism should improve this workspace"), treating all proposed workspace edits as falsifiable hypotheses1.

## **Diagnostic Decision Logic and Infrastructure Escalation**

When resolving a diagnosed friction item or recurring agent error, the workspace modification strategy must adhere to a strict eight-tier diagnostic priority hierarchy. Natural-language instruction additions represent the second-lowest priority intervention and must only be utilized when higher-level structural and deterministic interventions are technically infeasible.

### **The Eight-Tier Intervention Preference Hierarchy**

> 1. **Structural Change** (Highest Preference): Alter directory layouts, file paths, or workspace invariants to make the error physically or syntactically impossible5.
> 2. **Check**: Introduce an automated, deterministic verification script, linter, or test gate to catch the defect immediately upon occurrence5.
> 3. **Tool**: Encapsulate complex or multi-step execution commands into a simple, predictable wrapper script or tool interface5.
> 4. **Workflow**: Automate task progression and state transitions directly within the execution harness to remove manual decision points8.
> 5. **Retrieval**: Optimize dynamic context loading and indexing to ensure existing knowledge is surfaced when relevant, preventing instruction duplication5.
> 6. **Skill**: Create a modular, loadable procedural guide (SKILL.md) containing targeted standard operating procedures for specialized tasks3.
> 7. **Instruction**: Add a clear text rule to global configuration files—permitted only if tiers 1–6 are inapplicable and the rule is free of configuration smells5.
> 8. **Human Checkpoint** (Lowest Preference): Escalation to human operators, reserved strictly for genuine subjective ambiguities or high-risk authorization boundaries2.

### **Escalation Protocol: Knowledge to Infrastructure Migration**

The long-term maturity of a workspace relies on progressively migrating operational knowledge down the hierarchy toward automated infrastructure5. The desired operational progression shifts logic across six explicit stages:

> 1. Human remembers procedure (High cognitive friction).
> 2. Agent remembers instruction (High token cost).
> 3. Skill document encapsulates procedure (Modular loading)5.
> 4. Executable tool standardizes interface (Deterministic wrapper)8.
> 5. Automated check validates output (Automated gate)8.
> 6. Structural invariant enforces compliance (Zero decision burden)3.

This migration pattern ensures that as domain understanding stabilizes, operational cognitive load is permanently offloaded from the language model's context window into deterministic, zero-cost code hooks5.

### **Quantitative Prioritization Scoring**

Proposed workspace remodeling interventions are prioritized using an expected-value formulation that weighs operational friction against implementation complexity1:
![][image21]
Where:

* ![][image22]: Estimated occurrence count of the problem per 100 task executions.
* ![][image23]: Normalized scale (![][image24] to ![][image25]) measuring developer time lost per incident.
* ![][image26]: Probability (![][image27] to ![][image28]) that the error reoccurs without intervention.

High priority scores identify immediate remodeling candidates. However, high-risk interventions involving system permissions or structural directory overhauls must undergo explicit safety validation regardless of their numerical score8.

## **Governance Architecture, Evaluation Gates, and Safe Evolution**

Self-improving agent systems risk catastrophic drift, context poisoning, and recursive failure loops if allowed to modify their own workspace without external governance4. Safe evolution requires enforcing strict conceptual role separation, rigorous evaluation split boundaries, negative knowledge tracking, and progressive autonomy levels5.

### **Conceptual Role Separation Protocol**

The remodeling framework strictly segregates system responsibilities into seven distinct conceptual roles. Even when powered by the same underlying language model, these roles execute in isolated context windows with specialized prompts and permissions2:

* **Executor**: Runs operational tasks using current tools, context, and skills8.
* **Observer**: Logs execution traces, tool outputs, verifier results, and token costs without modifying state5.
* **Diagnostician**: Analyzes logged trajectories to identify root failure mechanisms and workspace friction points5.
* **Optimizer**: Formulates targeted, bounded workspace patches (Add/Delete/Replace) or infrastructure scripts9.
* **Evaluator**: Runs candidate workspace patches across isolated development and validation task sets5.
* **Gate**: Enforces strict score thresholds; accepts updates only if validation performance improves monotonically1.
* **History**: Persists execution outcomes, accepted changes, and rejected candidates into historical storage5.

### **Evaluation Isolation and Held-Out Task Splits**

To prevent the optimizer from overfitting workspace changes to specific historical failures, the evaluation harness maintains strict task isolation:
![][image32]

* **Development Tasks (![][image33])**: Used by the Diagnostician and Optimizer to analyze trajectories and draft candidates.
* **Validation Tasks (![][image34])**: Used by the Evaluator to gate candidates. A candidate workspace update is rejected if accuracy on ![][image34] drops or if token cost spikes beyond defined thresholds1.
* **Held-Out Tasks (![][image35])**: Reserved for periodic benchmark audits to measure true generalization and detect catastrophic forgetting across task domains1.

### **Negative Knowledge Management**

When a candidate workspace modification fails validation, it must not be discarded silently or appended directly to active instruction prompts4. Instead, the change is written to a dedicated negative knowledge store located at .workspace/rejected/.
![][image36]
The Optimizer inspects the rejected edit log during subsequent iteration cycles, preventing the system from repeatedly attempting identical or structurally similar failing edits1.

### **Progressive Autonomy Levels**

Workspace self-improvement must advance through eight explicit maturity levels. Systems are prohibited from skipping levels prior to demonstrating empirical stability.

| Autonomy Level | Operational Boundary | Human Involvement | Promotion Gate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Level 0** | Manual Observation | Human identifies all friction and manually edits files. | Baseline instrumentation pass. |
| **Level 1** | Telemetry Logging | Workspace automatically records execution traces and errors. | Verified log collection across 50 tasks. |
| **Level 2** | Automated Diagnosis | Agent parses logs and identifies root friction domains. | Diagnostic precision audit (\>90% accuracy). |
| **Level 3** | Guardrail Proposal | Agent generates candidate tools, checks, or skills for review. | Schema validation pass. |
| **Level 4** | Isolated Evaluation | Agent tests candidates in sandboxed worktrees against ![][image34]. | Zero regression on ![][image34]. |
| **Level 5** | Human-in-the-Loop | Human reviews validated candidates and manually approves merges. | 95% human acceptance rate across 20 edits. |
| **Level 6** | Low-Risk Auto-Promotion | Low-risk checks, formatters, and skill updates auto-promote. | Zero production regressions over 100 tasks. |
| **Level 7** | Full Autonomous Remodeling | Agent manages full workspace lifecycle; human handles edge cases. | Continuous held-out stability1. |

## **Strategic Remodeling Plan and Horizon Roadmap**

Applying the research synthesis, diagnostic decision logic, and governance constraints yields an actionable remodeling plan for the workspace environment.

### **Remodeling Hypotheses Matrix**

| Target Friction | Root Cause Analysis | Proposed Intervention Mechanism | Supporting Research Evidence | Risk & Impact | Implementation Cost | Validation Protocol |

### **Explicit Non-Changes Protocol**

Preserving system stability requires explicitly defining components that must remain unmodified during remodeling cycles:

| Protected Workspace Component | Strategic Rationale for Non-Modification | Risk of Alteration |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Core Security & Permission Policies** | Modifying authorization bounds directly risks privilege escalation or unsafe file access8. | Uncontrolled environment access and data destruction8. |
| **Base Test Harness Utilities** | Modifying the verifiers used to evaluate candidate changes invalidates benchmark integrity. | False positive updates via reward hacking or verifier corruption8. |
| **Stable Deterministic Libraries** | Re-implementing functioning third-party tools as agent prompts introduces non-determinism5. | Context bloat, hallucinated execution, and token cost escalation5. |
| **Raw Trajectory Log Storage** | Overwriting or truncating original rollout logs eliminates audit trails and negative memory. | Loss of historical failure evidence needed for optimization. |

### **Three-Horizon Implementation Roadmap**

#### **Horizon 1 — Foundational Low-Risk Infrastructure (Prerequisite Stage)**

* **Remodeling Boundaries**: Establish explicit file permissions, worktree isolation rules, and directory classifications8.
* **Configuration Smell Sanitation**: Audit existing AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files; strip Lint Leakage and extract specialized procedural text into modular skills/ files5.
* **Tool Interface Wrappers**: Encapsulate volatile multi-flag shell commands into single-purpose wrapper scripts inside tools/5.
* **Telemetry Instrumentation**: Deploy light background logging to record task success, retry counts, token usage, and tool failure traces8.

#### **Horizon 2 — Experimental Bounded Optimization (Gated Stage)**

* **Skill Optimization Engine**: Implement SkillOpt-style bounded textual edits (Add/Delete/Replace) constrained by an explicit edit budget ![][image4]9.
* **Validation Gate & Rejection Memory**: Instantiate automated evaluation gates on held-out validation tasks ![][image34] and populate .workspace/rejected/ logs1.
* **Trace-Driven Distillation**: Integrate Trace2Skill parallel error and success analysis loops to generate structured skill directories ![][image16] from execution traces7.
* **Workflow Automation**: Transition high-frequency multi-step sequences into harness-orchestrated workflows8.

#### **Horizon 3 — Advanced Autonomous Research (Maturity Stage)**

* **Joint Weight-Harness Co-Optimization**: Explore WHALE-style alternating adaptation, pairing model fine-tuning with harness evolution.
* **Continuous Online Compilation**: Deploy Evo-Harness style context-to-harness compilation over live enterprise task streams.
* **Causal Failure Attribution**: Implement advanced ReAct-style diagnostic sub-agents capable of deep root-cause localization across complex codebase snapshots2.
* **Autonomous Workspace Structural Evolution**: Enable safe, Level 6+ automated restructuring of directory layouts, skill trees, and verification suites guarded by continuous held-out safety benchmarks9.

### **Integrated Research Backlog**

To support long-term self-improvement, the agent must address fourteen fundamental research questions governing harness evolution:

> 1. **Target Abstraction Selection (R1)**: Determining when a lesson belongs in a linter rule, a script wrapper, a workflow template, or a skill document5.
> 2. **Learning Trigger Criteria (R2)**: Evaluating whether evolution should trigger on task failure, human correction, efficiency regressions, or periodic batch audits.
> 3. **Evidence Threshold Calibration (R3)**: Determining the minimum number of trajectory occurrences (![][image37] or ![][image25]) required before converting a failure pattern into a workspace guardrail6.
> 4. **Causal Failure Attribution (R4)**: Disentangling model inference randomness from infrastructure flaws, tool timeouts, and prompt ambiguities8.
> 5. **Regression Prevention & Holdout Integrity (R5)**: Guarding against catastrophic forgetting by testing candidates on held-out evaluation splits and recent task batches9.
> 6. **Skill Organization Topology (R6)**: Comparing flat skill directories against hierarchical, domain-routed skill trees3.
> 7. **Obsolete Knowledge Decay Protocols (R7)**: Establishing automated deprecation timers and usage-based garbage collection for unused skill files5.
> 8. **Retrieval Failure Detection (R8)**: Differentiating between missing skills and existing skills that failed to load due to poor indexing5.
> 9. **Positive Trajectory Synthesis (R9)**: Extracting high-efficiency procedures from successful traces without introducing volatile or non-generalizable shortcuts7.
> 10. **Human Effort Optimization (R10)**: Measuring human intervention time as a primary loss metric alongside accuracy and token cost8.
> 11. **Context Burden Controls (R11)**: Measuring the marginal accuracy return per active token in always-loaded configuration files5.
> 12. **Cross-Domain Generalization (R12)**: Verifying that workspace adaptations transfer across different model scales, families, and project types1.
> 13. **Dense Trajectory Feedback Integration (R13)**: Incorporating step-level verifier feedback rather than relying solely on final pass/fail labels.
> 14. **Safe Autonomous Remodeling Governance (R14)**: Decoupling proposal, evaluation, and promotion roles to guarantee auditability and revertibility.

By systematically working through this research backlog and adhering to validation-gated execution protocols, the workspace steadily evolves toward maximum reliability, reduced context overhead, and minimal reliance on human correction1.
